params.question: A tender, raised nodule is found on the episcleral surface. When a cotton-tipped swab is swept across it, the nodule moves freely. What does this mobility indicate?

answers.text: The nodule is a malignant melanoma requiring excision biopsy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Episcleral melanomas are exceedingly rare and present differently. A mobile, tender episcleral nodule in an inflamed eye is characteristic of nodular episcleritis.

answers.text: The inflammation involves the deep sclera and requires systemic immunosuppression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A scleral nodule is fixed and does not move on probing. Mobility indicates the inflammation is superficial — in the episcleral layer, not the sclera.

answers.text: The nodule is episcleral in origin, confirming nodular episcleritis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. An episcleral nodule sits in the loose connective tissue above the sclera and moves freely on probing. A scleral nodule, by contrast, is fixed because it is embedded in the dense collagenous scleral stroma.

answers.text: The conjunctival nodule is benign and needs no treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The nodule is episcleral, not conjunctival. While nodular episcleritis is indeed benign, it may require topical NSAIDs or oral flurbiprofen for symptom relief.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key distinction: an episcleral nodule moves freely when probed because the episclera is loose connective tissue, while a scleral nodule is fixed in the dense collagen of the sclera. Mobility = episcleritis.
Exactly right. The cotton-swab test exploits the loose episcleral tissue — an episcleral nodule moves freely, a scleral nodule does not. This bedside sign helps avoid unnecessary systemic workup.

interactions.label: A 30-year-old woman with confirmed simple episcleritis has persistent discomfort

params.question: A 30-year-old woman with confirmed simple episcleritis has persistent discomfort despite one week of lubricant drops and cool compresses. What is the next appropriate step?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Topical ketorolac, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drop, is the second step in the episcleritis management ladder when lubricants alone are insufficient.
Systemic corticosteroids are excessive for episcleritis. The condition is self-limiting and managed stepwise: lubricants, then topical NSAIDs, then oral flurbiprofen if needed.
Urgent rheumatology referral is appropriate for scleritis, not for an uncomplicated first episode of simple episcleritis. Referral is considered only for recurrent or bilateral episodes.
c-ANCA testing and immunosuppression are part of the scleritis workup for suspected granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Simple episcleritis does not warrant these investigations.

overallFeedback.feedback: The stepwise ladder is: lubricants → topical NSAID (ketorolac) → oral flurbiprofen. Episcleritis is self-limiting and managed conservatively. Systemic workup and immunosuppression are reserved for scleritis.
Well done. The management ladder for episcleritis is: lubricants and cool compresses → topical NSAID (ketorolac) → oral flurbiprofen 100 mg TDS for 2–3 weeks. The condition resolves within weeks.

interactions.label: Why is granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) considered the most critical syste

params.question: Why is granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) considered the most critical systemic association of scleritis that must not be missed?

answers.text: It is the most common systemic disease associated with scleritis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common association, accounting for 20–30% of scleritis cases. GPA is less common but far more dangerous if unrecognised.

answers.text: It causes a characteristic saddle-nose deformity that permanently disfigures the patient

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The saddle-nose deformity is a clinical clue that raises suspicion for GPA, but the critical concern is not disfigurement — it is the risk of fatal organ damage from necrotising vasculitis.

answers.text: Its necrotising vasculitis can cause fatal renal failure if left unrecognised

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. GPA deposits immune complexes in blood vessel walls. The same vasculitis that inflames the sclera can destroy the kidneys. A positive c-ANCA warrants immediate urine dipstick — microscopic haematuria signals glomerulonephritis requiring urgent nephrology referral.

answers.text: It is the only systemic condition that produces scleritis in both eyes simultaneously

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bilateral scleritis can occur with several systemic conditions, not just GPA. The urgency of recognising GPA lies in its potential for fatal renal and pulmonary vasculitis.

overallFeedback.feedback: GPA's necrotising vasculitis can cause fatal glomerulonephritis. That is why it must not be missed. Remember: c-ANCA positive → urine dipstick → nephrology referral if microscopic blood is found.

Exactly. GPA is critical because the same vasculitis affecting the sclera can silently destroy the kidneys. The bedside rule: c-ANCA positive → dipstick the urine → if haematuria, urgent nephrology referral.

params.question: A 52-year-old man presents with deep boring eye pain that wakes him at night. He has a saddle-nose deformity. Phenylephrine 2.5% produces no blanching. Which combination of findings drives the urgency of his referral?

answers.text: Non-blanching redness and mild aching confirm nodular episcleritis, warranting outpatient review in two weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Non-blanching redness indicates scleritis, not episcleritis. Deep boring nocturnal pain is inconsistent with episcleritis, which causes only mild aching and never disturbs sleep.

answers.text: Non-blanching redness confirms scleritis; the saddle-nose deformity raises suspicion for GPA, requiring same-day rheumatology and nephrology referral

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Non-blanching = scleritis. Saddle-nose deformity is a red flag for GPA, a necrotising vasculitis. This combination demands urgent same-day rheumatology and nephrology assessment to exclude life-threatening renal involvement.

answers.text: The boring pain and non-blanching suggest bacterial scleritis, requiring urgent intravenous antibiotics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Scleritis is an autoimmune vasculitis, not an infection. The deep boring pain reflects immune-mediated scleral inflammation. The saddle-nose deformity points to GPA, not a bacterial cause.

answers.text: The saddle-nose deformity is incidental; scleritis alone requires oral NSAIDs and routine rheumatology referral within two weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A saddle-nose deformity in the context of scleritis is a strong clinical clue for GPA, not an incidental finding. Treating this as routine risks missing a life-threatening necrotising vasculitis with renal involvement.

overallFeedback.feedback: Follow the algorithm: phenylephrine non-blanching = scleritis. Saddle-nose deformity = red flag for GPA. Together, these mandate same-day emergency referral to rheumatology and nephrology — not routine outpatient care.

Well analysed. The algorithm: non-blanching → scleritis → saddle-nose raises GPA → order the full panel including c-ANCA → same-day rheumatology and nephrology. Urgency scales with severity, and this patient sits at the highest tier.
